channel.title: Investigating Chronos-2
channel.description: A measured study of a time-series foundation model on the M5 benchmark: a gradient-boosted baseline, the foundation model, and what it takes to find out whether the remaining headroom is reachable.

item.title: Have we reached a ceiling?
item.description:
The previous post ended flat. One lever was left: treat different items differently. Fine-tune per group, cross-learn inside a group, one model per group.

That lever has a precondition, and it is testable beforhand. For a static grouping to help, difficulty has to be a stable property of an item. If the items that are hard this week are not the ones that were hard last week, it means the error cannot be decreased by finding a different setup for the worst items, as it is akin to a transient effect.

This post answers that, and then keeps narrowing. Difficulty is a stable property of the item. Two thirds of it is volume, which needs no clustering to exploit.

The panel

To analyse the difficulty’s, we divide the time horizon in twenty-four origins, one week apart, in order to score over 7-day non-overlapping windows (non-overlapping matters: with overlapping windows the correlation between consecutive origins would be partly an artefact of shared days). The restricted model used in this post is the zero-shot one at the context length chosen for days 1–7 (see the previous post), predicting 7 days ahead only — the fine-tuned model is disqualified here, because walking its test-origin checkpoint backwards would let it see the future of every earlier window.

The dataset sample is the same as in the previous post, and amongst the 494 series that are scorable at least once, 138 are scorable at every origin, so they constitute our panel. This way, every item in the panel has its difficulty measured on the same set of weeks. The figure below plots each of the selected item’s relative difficulty at each forecast origin:

Show the code 
order = np.argsort(result.alpha)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4.5))
image = ax.imshow(panel.x[order], aspect="auto", cmap="RdYlBu_r", interpolation="nearest",
                  vmin=np.quantile(panel.x, 0.02), vmax=np.quantile(panel.x, 0.98))
ax.set_xlabel("origin (one week apart, oldest left)")
ax.set_ylabel("item, sorted by average difficulty")
ax.set_xticks(range(0, n_origins, 4))
ax.set_xticklabels([str(panel.origins[i]) for i in range(0, n_origins, 4)],
                   rotation=45, ha="right")
ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, label="log WQL", shrink=0.85)
plt.show()

Though we can suspect an at least mild correlation between weeks, as the graph suggests some horizontal lines, the error ditribution and origin needs to be properly assessed. So we split the error of each (item, origin), written , cell in four ways:

where is the global mean; is the item — by construction the only part a static grouping could exploit; is the week - are some weeks are hard for everyone? What is left splits further into a part that survives to the next origin (persistent), a part that does not (transient), and the sampling noise of the cell itself, measured from the odd and even days of each window. It is all contained within .

Our task now is to scan the distribution for clusters and continuums.

Does the estimator work?

Before touching the real panel, I ran our scaning method on a simulated one with known components, at the same panel size and noise level. The results are:

Show the code 
control, planted = simulate_panel(n_series=250, n_origins=N_ORIGINS, seed=SEED)
recovered = decompose(control).shares()
components = ["series", "origin", "persistent", "transient", "noise"]
planted_pct = np.array([100 * planted[c] for c in components])
recovered_pct = np.array([100 * recovered["series_adjusted" if c == "series" else c]
                          for c in components])

# The same estimator, on a panel whose only stable signal is an AR(1) drift.
DRIFT_GRID = [0.0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.75, 0.85, 0.92, 0.97]
drift = []
for drift_rho in DRIFT_GRID:
    simulated, truth = simulate_panel(n_series=250, n_origins=N_ORIGINS, rho=drift_rho,
                                      sd_series=0.0, sd_persistent=0.33, seed=0)
    split = decompose(simulated).shares()
    drift.append((100 * split["series_adjusted"], 100 * split["persistent"],
                  100 * (truth["series"] + truth["persistent"])))
drift_item, drift_persistent, drift_planted = (np.array(v) for v in zip(*drift))
drift_total_error = float(np.abs(drift_item + drift_persistent - drift_planted).max())

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))

ax = axes[0]
order = np.argsort(planted_pct)
y = np.arange(len(components))
ax.barh(y + 0.19, planted_pct[order], height=0.36, color=plots.GRID_COLOR, label="planted")
ax.barh(y - 0.19, recovered_pct[order], height=0.36, color=plots.MAIN_COLOR,
        label="recovered")
for row, left, right in zip(y, planted_pct[order], recovered_pct[order]):
    ax.text(max(left, right) + 1.2, row, f"{left:.0f} / {right:.0f}", va="center",
            fontsize=8, color=plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR)
ax.set_yticks(y); ax.set_yticklabels([components[i] for i in order])
ax.set_xlim(0, max(planted_pct.max(), recovered_pct.max()) * 1.25)
ax.set_xlabel("share of the variance budget (%)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, frameon=False, loc="lower right")
ax.set_title("the estimator recovers what was planted", fontsize=9, loc="left",
             color=plots.TEXT_COLOR)

ax = axes[1]
ax.plot(DRIFT_GRID, drift_planted, color=plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR, linestyle="--",
        linewidth=1.4, label="planted (item + persistent)")
ax.plot(DRIFT_GRID, drift_item + drift_persistent, color=plots.TEXT_COLOR, marker="o",
        markersize=4, linewidth=1.8, label="recovered, the two together")
ax.plot(DRIFT_GRID, drift_item, color=plots.MAIN_COLOR, marker="o", markersize=4,
        linewidth=1.5, label="recovered as item")
ax.plot(DRIFT_GRID, drift_persistent, color=plots.MAIN_COLOR, marker="o", markersize=4,
        linewidth=1.5, linestyle=":", label="recovered as persistent")
ax.set_xlabel("autocorrelation of the planted drift")
ax.set_ylabel("share of the budget (%)")
ax.set_title("but not which of the two it is", fontsize=9, loc="left",
             color=plots.TEXT_COLOR)
ax.legend(fontsize=7.5, frameon=False, loc="upper left")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The left subfigure proves we can trust the method for recovering error shares. However, the right subfigure is the method’s one real limit. In case of a slow drift, it is hard to tell from a constant difficulty over six months, and the estimator divides it badly: at an autocorrelation of 0.97, a drift with no constant item effect planted anywhere comes back as a 16% item effect. The total it does get right, to within 1.4 points everywhere on the grid.

The takeaway is that the item share answers could a grouping fitted once and left alone help, and the sum answers is there anything stable at all, even if it has to be refitted.

Where the error lives

Now what does our method yield for our real pannel?

Show the code 
intervals = bootstrap_shares(panel, n_draws=1000, seed=SEED)
md(pl.DataFrame([
    {"component": name, "share %": 100 * shares[key],
     "CI low %": 100 * intervals[key][0], "CI high %": 100 * intervals[key][1]}
    for name, key in [("item (raw)", "series"),
                      ("item (bias-adjusted)", "series_adjusted"),
                      ("week", "origin"),
                      ("item x week", "interaction"),
                      ("  - persistent", "persistent"),
                      ("  - transient", "transient"),
                      ("  - sampling noise", "noise"),
                      ("stable (item + persistent)", "stable")]]), digits=1)

Two numbers summarise the section.

  1. The identity of the item accounts for 42% of the variance in log WQL once the noise inside each is removed.
  2. the week accounts for 2% — there are essentially no weeks that are hard for everybody. Difficulty mostly comes from the item.

Most of what remains is sampling noise, which is what forecasting 7-day windows of items selling a few units a week buys you. That matters for the next section, in which we try to findt he same result with a different tool.

Two instruments, one answer

The previous section gave us our conclusion. But a decomposition is a model, and a model can be wrong. Thereofer, we may want to use something like rank agreement to confirm our findings: it is a direct measurement of consistency, with no assumptions behind it:

Show the code 
ranks = rank_agreement(panel, decile=0.10)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))
ax = axes[0]
values = ranks["consecutive"]
ax.plot(range(1, len(values) + 1), values, color=plots.MAIN_COLOR, marker="o", markersize=4)
ax.axhline(ranks["consecutive_median"], color=plots.TEXT_COLOR, linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
ax.axhspan(-0.5, 0.5, color=plots.GRID_COLOR, alpha=0.6, zorder=0)
ax.text(0.98, 0.04, "|rho| < 0.5: 'weak' for test-retest", transform=ax.transAxes,
        ha="right", va="bottom", color=plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR, fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylim(-1, 1)
ax.set_xlabel("pair of consecutive origins")
ax.set_ylabel("Spearman of the difficulty ranking")
ax = axes[1]
first, last = panel.x[:, 0], panel.x[:, -1]
ax.scatter(first, last, s=10, color=plots.MAIN_COLOR, alpha=0.6)
limits = [min(first.min(), last.min()), max(first.max(), last.max())]
ax.plot(limits, limits, color=plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR, linewidth=1)
ax.set_xlabel(f"log WQL at {panel.origins[0]}")
ax.set_ylabel(f"... at {panel.origins[-1]}")
ax.text(0.03, 0.95, f"Spearman {ranks['first_vs_last']:+.2f}", transform=ax.transAxes,
        va="top", color=plots.TEXT_COLOR)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Immediately, the median of +0.52 between consecutive origins looks like a weak agreement, challenging the previous section’s result (test–retest conventions call anything under 0.5 weak). Taken at face value, the two sections seem to disagree: a large item effect, and a ranking that only half holds.

But they don’t. The decomposition predicts the rank correlation, and this prediction can be written down from the variance shares alone:

  1. Within one origin the week effect is a constant and does not touch the across-items ranking, so the spread of the measured error at a single origin is
  2. The covariance between two consecutive origins keeps only the parts that survive the step from the previous value, .
  3. Their ratio is the correlation the model expects anyone to observe. Six months apart the persistent part has decayed and only remains.
  4. So rank correlation is equal to .

Therefore noise enters only in the denominator, and being responsible for around 40% of cell’s error, so it halves this correlation rate, despite being unrepresentative of the actual phenomenon.

So divide instead by the reliable part of a cell — everything except the sampling noise — and what comes out is the correlation between the underlying difficulties rather than between their noisy estimates:

Show the code 
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

v_alpha = shares["series_adjusted"]
v_pers, v_trans, v_noise = shares["persistent"], shares["transient"], shares["noise"]
cell_variance = v_alpha + v_pers + v_trans + v_noise
reliability = (v_alpha + v_pers + v_trans) / cell_variance

attenuation = pl.DataFrame([
    {"quantity": "consecutive origins",
     "predicted": (v_alpha + v_pers) / cell_variance,
     "observed": ranks["consecutive_median"],
     "noise-corrected": (v_alpha + v_pers) / (v_alpha + v_pers + v_trans)},
    {"quantity": "first vs last origin",
     "predicted": v_alpha / cell_variance,
     "observed": ranks["first_vs_last"],
     "noise-corrected": v_alpha / (v_alpha + v_pers + v_trans)},
])

predicted = attenuation["predicted"].to_numpy()
observed = attenuation["observed"].to_numpy()
corrected = attenuation["noise-corrected"].to_numpy()
rows = np.arange(attenuation.height)[::-1]          # first quantity on top

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 2.9),
                         gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.7, 1]})

ax = axes[0]
for row, p, o, c in zip(rows, predicted, observed, corrected):
    ax.plot([min(p, o), c], [row, row], color=plots.GRID_COLOR, linewidth=7,
            solid_capstyle="round", zorder=1)
    ax.scatter(p, row, s=80, facecolor="white", edgecolor=plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR,
               linewidth=1.6, zorder=3)
    ax.scatter(o, row, s=55, color=plots.MAIN_COLOR, zorder=4)
    ax.scatter(c, row, s=80, color=plots.TEXT_COLOR, marker="D", zorder=3)
ax.set_yticks(rows)
ax.set_yticklabels(attenuation["quantity"].to_list())
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, attenuation.height - 0.3)
ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
ax.axvline(0.5, color=plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR, linestyle=":", linewidth=1, zorder=0)
ax.text(0.49, -0.62, "0.5: 'weak' for test-retest", ha="right", va="bottom",
        color=plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR, fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlabel("Spearman correlation of the difficulty ranking")
ax.legend(handles=[
    Line2D([], [], marker="o", linestyle="", markerfacecolor="white",
           markeredgecolor=plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR, markersize=9, label="predicted"),
    Line2D([], [], marker="o", linestyle="", color=plots.MAIN_COLOR,
           markersize=8, label="observed"),
    Line2D([], [], marker="D", linestyle="", color=plots.TEXT_COLOR,
           markersize=8, label="noise-corrected"),
], loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0, 1.02), ncol=3, frameon=False, fontsize=8)

ax = axes[1]
residual = observed - predicted
span = float(np.abs(residual).max()) * 2.4
ax.barh(rows, residual, color=plots.MAIN_COLOR, height=0.38)
ax.axvline(0, color=plots.TEXT_COLOR, linewidth=1)
for row, value in zip(rows, residual):
    offset = 0.05 * span if value > 0 else -0.05 * span
    ax.text(value + offset, row, f"{value:+.3f}", va="center",
            ha="left" if value > 0 else "right", color=plots.TEXT_COLOR, fontsize=9)
ax.set_yticks(rows); ax.set_yticklabels([]); ax.tick_params(left=False)
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, attenuation.height - 0.3)
ax.set_xlim(-span, span)
ax.set_xlabel("observed − predicted")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The figure shows the difference between the original blunt ruler and the more faithfull one: the grey bar is what the bluntness costs, and the underlying difficulty ordering is stable at 0.86 - confirming the previous section’s strong conclusion.

The residuals are reassuring (right pannel): they fall on opposite sides of zero. A systematic error in the variance model would push both the same way.

The six-month row says something further. Nearly all of the long-run agreement is the term — the persistent part has decayed by then — so is behaving like a genuinely fixed property of the item rather than a slow drift. If we remember section “Does the estimator work?”’s warning, we see that we are safe.

Most of it is volume

A large item share isn’t the end of our analysis. WQL is scale-free, so a dependence on volume would not be an artefact of units — it would be a statement about predictability: “an item selling a third of a unit a day has an irreducibly high relative error, and that is a permanent property of the item”.

That distinction decides what is worth. If it is a function of volume, then “group the items by difficulty” means “bucket them by volume”, which needs no clustering and which the forecaster reads off the history unaided.

One correction is mandatory though. The sampling noise of a 7-day window is itself strongly volume-dependent, so low-volume items have their inflated more — which would manufacture exactly the relationship I am testing for. A global bias adjustment cannot fix a bias that differs per item, so I measure each item’s noise from its own odd and even days and remove it individually.

Show the code 
volume_record = RECORD["stable_vs_volume"]
rho = volume_record["spearman"]
md(pl.DataFrame([
    {"removed": "nothing (raw item effect)", "Spearman with alpha": None,
     "item share of the budget %": 100 * volume_record["share_raw"]},
    {"removed": "each item's own measured noise", "Spearman with alpha": None,
     "item share of the budget %": 100 * volume_record["share_noise_corrected"]},
    {"removed": "+ log volume", "Spearman with alpha": rho["log volume"],
     "item share of the budget %": None},
    {"removed": "+ zero-day share", "Spearman with alpha": rho["zero-day share"],
     "item share of the budget %": None},
    {"removed": "+ both covariates", "Spearman with alpha": None,
     "item share of the budget %": 100 * volume_record["share_after_covariates"]},
]), digits=2)
Show the code 
prior = SALES.filter(pl.col("date") <= ORIGINS[0], ~pl.col("is_missing"))
profile = (prior.group_by("id")
           .agg(pl.col("sales").mean().alias("mean_daily"),
                (pl.col("sales") == 0).mean().alias("zero_share")))
aligned = pl.DataFrame({"id": panel.ids}).join(profile, on="id", how="left")
log_volume = np.log(np.maximum(aligned["mean_daily"].to_numpy(), 1e-3))

from m5_chronos2.persistence import series_noise
precision = 1 / np.maximum(series_noise(panel), np.percentile(series_noise(panel), 5))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))
for ax, x, label in [(axes[0], log_volume, "log mean units sold per day"),
                     (axes[1], aligned["zero_share"].to_numpy(), "share of zero-sale days")]:
    ax.scatter(x, result.alpha, s=6 + 40 * precision / precision.max(),
               color=plots.MAIN_COLOR, alpha=0.55, edgecolor="none")
    ax.set_xlabel(label)
    ax.set_ylabel(r"$\alpha_i$  (stable difficulty)")
axes[0].text(0.03, 0.06, f"Spearman {rho['log volume']:+.2f}", transform=axes[0].transAxes,
             color=plots.TEXT_COLOR)
axes[1].text(0.03, 0.94, f"Spearman {rho['zero-day share']:+.2f}",
             transform=axes[1].transAxes, va="top", color=plots.TEXT_COLOR)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

So we obtain a good linear tendency that confirms the initial statement: volume and sparsity together explain 63% of the stable difficulty. Two details matter for reading that.

They are not two different readings. Volume alone reaches the same 63%, soadding the zero-day share moves nothing. At a Spearman of +0.71 with and a near-mechanical relationship to volume on data that is two thirds zeros, sparsity is a second view of the same quantity, not an independent factor.

And the noise channel is not what is driving it. Wwe already justified that a noisier estimate of the same underlying error could have a different expectation. The direct test is to ask how much of the measurement noise itself explains: it reaches 0.63 as a Spearman against 0.77 for volume, and 34% of the variance against 63%. If the volume relationship were an artefact of the noise level, the noise level would be the proximate cause and the stronger correlate. It is the weaker one, by a clear margin.

So two thirds of the stable item effect is a sort on a number already in the history, and one third is not: 15.6% of the whole error budget, against 2.0% for the week and 11.5% for everything transient. It is the largest addressable term left, and the only one a grouping could earn its keep on. So I tried to find some root cause of its effect.

Is the rest of it in the weekly shape?

The residual is real. The question is where to look for it, and I tried to do so in the weekly shape — the share of a week falling on each weekday. Shape is worth testing because it is a different axis from volume by construction. But that is also why the link cannot be assumed: the dominant component of the item effect has been removed from the object on purpose, so whether anything of the item effect is left in that object is an open empirical question — and the cheapest one available, because it decides whether a clustering of the shape space is worth building at all.

Could the residual be understood from categorizing items based on their weekly shape? Each week is normalised to 1, the weeks are pooled, and the result is a 7-vector summing to 1, so how much an item sells drops out and only when it sells remains.

Let’s see what that looks like:

Show the code 
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.8), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.3]})
ax = axes[0]
generator = np.random.default_rng(0)
for index in generator.choice(len(X), size=min(40, len(X)), replace=False):
    ax.plot(range(WEEKDAYS), X[index], color=plots.MAIN_COLOR, alpha=0.18, linewidth=1)
ax.plot(range(WEEKDAYS), X.mean(axis=0), color=plots.TEXT_COLOR, linewidth=2.5)
ax.axhline(1 / WEEKDAYS, color=plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR, linestyle=":", linewidth=1)
ax.text(0.02, 1 / WEEKDAYS, " a flat week", va="bottom", ha="left",
        color=plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR, fontsize=8)
ax.set_xticks(range(WEEKDAYS)); ax.set_xticklabels(DAY_NAMES)
ax.set_ylabel("share of the week")
ax = axes[1]
weekend = X[:, 5] + X[:, 6]
image = ax.imshow(X[np.argsort(weekend)], aspect="auto", cmap="RdYlBu_r",
                  interpolation="nearest", vmin=np.quantile(X, 0.02),
                  vmax=np.quantile(X, 0.98))
ax.set_xticks(range(WEEKDAYS)); ax.set_xticklabels(DAY_NAMES)
ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_ylabel("item, sorted by weekend share")
ax.grid(False)
fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, label="share of the week", shrink=0.9)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The left and right plot reveal these weekly patterns with different perspectives, but they both seem to suggest that we are facing a continuum - which wouldn’t give us any new way to track down the residual error.

In case the construction isn’t clear, I animated it (with manim) on planted archetypes: four invented weekly shapes, scattered and then redrawn as counts at the items’ real weekly totals. It is synthetic data that shows what the space is and what genuine structure in it would look like, which is what makes the measurement below legible either way.

So I regress on volume, sparsity and the per-item noise level, then add the six free shape coordinates (the sum adds up to one, so the seventh is derived from the first six) and ask what they buy. I defined three rules:

  • Shape is measured on history strictly before the panel’s first origin. A profile computed over the scored windows would be partly measured on what it predicts.
  • Six extra regressors explain variance by construction — about of what is left. That is removed in expectation, and a permutation test gives the distribution instead of the expectation. The shuffle is stratified by volume, so the null keeps whatever relationship shape has with volume and destroys only its link to difficulty. Permuting freely would break the shape–volume relationship too, make the null easier to beat, and bias the test toward finding an effect.
  • Shape is itself measured with error, and error in a predictor attenuates what it explains toward zero — the mirror image of the attenuation above. So the increment is reported both as measured and divided by the shape’s own reliability, as an upper bound on what a perfectly measured shape could contribute.
Show the code 
bridge = RECORD["shape_vs_alpha"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.4), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.15]})

ax = axes[0]
bars = [("observed", bridge["increment"], plots.MAIN_COLOR),
        ("null median", bridge["null_median"], plots.GRID_COLOR),
        ("null 95th pct", bridge["null_p95"], plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR),
        ("ceiling if shape\nwere perfect", bridge["increment_disattenuated"],
         plots.TEXT_COLOR)]
ax.barh([b[0] for b in bars], [100 * b[1] for b in bars],
        color=[b[2] for b in bars], height=0.6)
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlabel("share of the stable difficulty that shape explains (%)")
ax.text(0.97, 0.08, f"p = {bridge['p_value']:.2f}", transform=ax.transAxes,
        ha="right", color=plots.TEXT_COLOR)

ax = axes[1]
ax.bar(range(WEEKDAYS), bridge["spearman_per_weekday"], color=plots.MAIN_COLOR, width=0.6)
ax.axhline(0, color=plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR, linewidth=1)
ax.set_xticks(range(WEEKDAYS)); ax.set_xticklabels(DAY_NAMES)
ax.set_ylim(-0.4, 0.4)
ax.set_ylabel(r"Spearman with $\alpha_i$")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Conclusion: the weekly shape carries essentially none of the error. The observed increment is 0.7% of the stable difficulty, below the null’s 95th percentile of 1.5%, at p = 0.15 over 1000 permutations in 10 volume strata. Shape explains less than a typical volume-preserving shuffle does.

And the result is bounded. The profile’s own split-half reliability on these items is 0.44, so a perfectly measured weekly shape could account for at most 1.5% — the fourth bar from the figure. There is no version of this measurement, however much the ruler improves, in which the weekly shape reaches the 15.6% that is still on the item.

The per-weekday correlations on the right never leave ±0.16, so no single weekday carries difficulty either.

Where this leaves the question

What we established about the error’s origin. 42% of the variance in log WQL sits on the identity of the item against 2% on the week, with high week-to-week stability - and even six-month stability. Of that, 63% is volume — a continuous covariate already present in the history, needing no clustering. The 15.6% that remains is item-specific, stable, and not in the weekly shape, at a ceiling of 1.5%. The shape space is calendar-anchored, and its measurability rises monotonically with volume.

Leads that ares till open. Whether that residual is organised at all, and on what axis. Candidates I have not tested are, for example: burstiness and volatility, lifecycle stage, promotion and price response, intermittency structure beyond the zero-day share…

What it means for our model’s performances. We started this post by wondering if we could leverage some hidden structure’s correlation with prediction difficulty. And we did find such structure: however the irony is that it is inherently already accessible and used by Chronos2. Therefore, we are back to the same stage as in the end of the previous post, though our understanding is much greater.

item.title: The baseline: XGBoost
item.description:
Testing our foundation model only makes sense when putting it against something else. So I began by building the reference it would have to beat: a feature-engineered gradient-boosting model, in the tradition that won M5, inspired by a public top-4% solution.

The result worth stating up front is how little the feature engineering buys over the “mean of the last 28 days” elementary model. That is not a criticism of the solution reproduced — I reduced it to a single XGBoost model where the original used LightGBM - but by seeing this fully engineered XGBoost version as a canonical representative of traditional machine learning techniques, it makes the comparison in the next post all the more interesting.

The dataset

One target value per series per day: units of one item sold in one Walmart store. History runs 2011-01-29 to 2016-05-22, 1,941 days, 30,490 series. The task is to predict 28 days ahead.

I work throughout on a frozen random sample of 500 series, drawn once and saved, so every number in these three posts comes from the same items. The sample is for practical computing power reasons, as the whole study was made on a 10 year old laptop.

Show the code 
on_sale = SALES.filter(~pl.col("is_missing"))
per_series = on_sale.group_by("id", "cat_id").agg(
    pl.col("sales").mean().alias("mean_daily"),
    (pl.col("sales") == 0).mean().alias("zero_share"),
)
median_zero = per_series["zero_share"].median()
median_daily = per_series["mean_daily"].median()

fig, (left, right) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.2))
left.hist(per_series["zero_share"].to_numpy(), bins=np.linspace(0, 1, 21),
          color=plots.MAIN_COLOR, edgecolor="white")
left.set_xlabel("share of on-sale days with zero sales")
left.set_ylabel("number of series")
for category, colour in plots.CATEGORY_COLORS.items():
    values = per_series.filter(pl.col("cat_id") == category)["mean_daily"].to_numpy()
    right.hist(values, bins=np.logspace(-2, 2.5, 28), histtype="step",
               linewidth=2, color=colour, label=category)
right.set_xscale("log")
right.set_xlabel("mean units sold per day (log scale)")
right.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The median sells of the averaged series is 0.55 units a day, and the median share of days a series is on the shelf but isn’t sold is 66%. Figure 1 proves that this median is fairly representative, so we are dealing with mostly near zero series. Two consequences run through everything that follows.

First, a zero is information, not a gap. There is only one exception: the days before an item’s first price in sell_prices.csv, when it was not on the shelf at all. Those are dropped from every history (I tracked this effect by only keeping values from where a price tag has been attributed to an item). Everything else is a real zero — the item was available and nobody bought it — and it is part of what the forecast has to get right.

Second, periods of zero sales are common, so if our evaluation metric is a percentage error, we need to filter the series. This could reduce further our sample size.

The harness comes first

I set two forecast origins, for two different purposes:

A (series, window) pair is scored only if it clears three conditions:

  1. at least 56 days (arbitrary, but reasonable) on sale before the origin
  2. no missing day inside the window
  3. at least one unit sold in the window.

The third is necessary — WMAPE and WQL divide by the window’s total, so a series that sells nothing has no defined error (cf. paragraph above).

The surviving list is frozen to disk. A roster that quietly changes between models turns every later comparison into a comparison of populations, which would be undesirable.

Of the 500 sampled series, 473 are scorable on the validation window and 485 on the test window. It so happens that every exclusion is the no-sale condition.

Five metrics, and what each is for

metric definition what it is for
MAE mean of error in units sold
WMAPE scale-free, survives zeros: the headline
P90 90th percentile of the bad days
WQL mean over of the whole forecast distribution
RQL the point forecast, with over-prediction priced at four times under-prediction

is the quantile loss on a forecast : when , when . WQL applies it to each quantile forecast in turn, and is a staple scoring rule. For distributional models, refers to the median value. RQL applies to the point forecast instead, because the asymmetry is meant to price the cost of acting on the number the model puts forward. Scoring it on the 0.2 quantile column would reward a model for submitting a deliberately low number: over-predicting costs 4 times more than under-predicting. This signal matters in practice as retailers want to know whether following the predictions means risking over production (more costly then under production). If not mentioned, all sums run over scored (series, day) pairs, never averaged per series and then averaged again.

One remark for the next post: for a model that only gives a point forecast, every quantile column is a copy of it, and WQL collapses to WMAPE/100. A probabilistic model can beat that number only by saying something true about its own uncertainty. So WQL is not a fair axis for comparing a point model with a distributional one; MAE, WMAPE, P90 and RQL are. However WQL will be our main decider for a batch of distributional models.

Three naive baselines

Always zero, repeat-last-week, and the mean of the last 28 days. On intermittent data the first is not absurd, and the third is a genuinely strong competitor.

Show the code 
baselines = ["zero", "seasonal_naive", "moving_average_28d"]
md(rename_models(table_of(baselines, "validation"))
   .select(["model", "n_series"] + metrics.METRICS).sort("WMAPE"))

Note the ordering: repeating last week is barely better than predicting nothing at all, while a flat 28-day mean removes about a fifth of the error. After all, on series this sparse the exact weekly pattern of a single item is mostly noise, and averaging it away beats reproducing it.

RQL inverts the ranking — the zero forecast wins it outright, 20 against 39. The metric is doing its job, by showing how low volume the real values mostly are.

The features

Rather than invent a feature set, which consumes a lot of time (and insight!), I reproduced one that is public and well ranked: btrotta/kaggle-m5 (predict.py) is a top-4% M5 solution. It builds fifty-two features in four families:

  • the series’ own past — lags 1 to 7, means of the last 7/14/28 days, running mean and variance overall and per weekday;
  • the same, two levels up — the item’s department in its store, and the item across all stores, so a thin series borrows the shape of its neighbours;
  • calendar — weekday, month, SNAP benefit days, and an “event uplift” measured as mean sales n days after an event minus the same weekday a week later;
  • price — the current price and its change over 7 and 14 days, plus days since first sale.

The strategy is direct: 28 models, one per forecast day. The model for day k sees sales only up to the origin, with its lag features shifted k days further back, so no forecast is ever fed back as an input and nothing in the window leaks.

I strayed from the original in five places, deliberately:

  • XGBoost instead of LightGBM, with the closest equivalent settings (easier to run, and the core principle);
  • training on the 500-series sample rather than all 30,490 — though the department and item features are still computed on all of them;
  • boosting rounds chosen by early stopping on the last 28 days before the origin, where the original stops on the window it then reports;
  • the event uplift implemented as intended rather than as coded;
  • missing days are defined by the price file.

What it buys

Show the code 
models = baselines + ["xgboost_btrotta"]
XGB_TABLE = pl.concat([
    table_of(models, role).with_columns(pl.lit(role).alias("window"))
    for role in ("validation", "test")
])

def wmape(model, window):
    """One WMAPE cell of this table, so the prose below cannot drift away from it."""
    return XGB_TABLE.filter(pl.col("model") == model,
                            pl.col("window") == window)["WMAPE"].item()

md(rename_models(XGB_TABLE)
   .select(["window", "model", "n_series"] + metrics.METRICS).sort("window", "WMAPE"))
Show the code 
fig, axes = plots.plot_by_bucket(table_of(models, "validation", by="horizon_bucket"),
                                 metrics.METRICS)
plt.show()

With the 52 features, we get 0.8 WMAPE points on validation, 1.2 on test. In relative terms that is a cut of 1.0% in WMAPE on validation and 1.6% on test — the same percentages for MAE, which cannot differ — and set against the fifth of the error the 28-day mean had already removed on its own, the fifty-two features add only 4% of that ground on validation and 5% on test. The horizon view says where that comes from — for all metrics except P90, the two are nearly tied after the first week. So the first week is especially to the model’s advantage: it is where it should indeed be at its strongest.

The per-series view is blunter.

Show the code 
def per_series_wql(model):
    return metrics.score(scored(model, "validation"), by="id").select(
        "id", pl.col("WQL").alias(f"WQL_{model}"))

volume = (scored("xgboost_btrotta", "validation")
          .group_by("id").agg(pl.col("y").sum().alias("volume")))
comparison = (per_series_wql("moving_average_28d")
              .join(per_series_wql("xgboost_btrotta"), on="id")
              .join(volume, on="id"))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.5))
share = plots.index_plot(ax, comparison, "WQL",
                         "moving_average_28d", "xgboost_btrotta", order_by="volume")
plt.show()

XGBoost has the lower WQL (ie WMAPE) on 43% of series. It loses on the majority of items and still wins overall, because the items it wins on are the ones that sell. Therefore, it reacts better to changes. The core difficulty of the dataset really is how low the values are.

What the baseline settles

Three things carry into the next post.

The dataset’s difficulty. As we showed, this prediction problem is made much harder by the low volume of the series (which are integer values, so it isn’t just a matter of scaling).

A number to beat. WMAPE 78.8 on validation, 76.4 on test (pooled over the whole forecast horizon) — and the honest framing is that most of that was already available from a 28-day mean (79.6 and 77.6), despite how rough of an estimate it is.

A caveat. XGBoost is trained on squared error, so it estimates a conditional mean. On absolute-error metrics the optimal point forecast is the median, so any model that returns a median starts with a structural advantage on MAE and WMAPE that has nothing to do with forecasting better. However, Chronos-2 returns a median. Moreover, because it is distributional, Chronos-2 has a slight edge. When looking at WQL, without regards to if the derived point forecast is actually better. So in case of a tight match, strong conclusions would be unfaithful.

Next page

item.title: Chronos-2, knob by knob
item.description:
The previous post left me a number to beat: WMAPE 78.8 on the validation window. Intros post I hand Chronos-2 the sales history and nothing else.

What the model is

Chronos-2 is a pre-trained T5-style encoder for forecasting of about 120M parameters. It cuts the history into patches of 16 days, embeds each as a vector, and emits the quantiles of the whole horizon in a single forward pass — no token vocabulary, no step-by-step decoding, and the horizon length is an input, contrary to an LLM application of the same architecture. The derived point forecast for the study is the median.

The original project behind Chronos-2 (created by an Amazon research team) was to train an LLM to understand the “language” of time series, and thus generate the most probable future. But building a finite vocabulary for real numbers turned out to be inefficient for out-of-the-box applications, which led the team to strip both the first and the last layer of the architecture to keep only the calculus layers in between - which inherently handle real numbers.

I chose M5 partly because Chronos-2 has no training leakage on it, so any zero-shot number be authentic.

In this post, out-of-the-box will mean: no covariates, no fine-tuning, cross-learning off, and default context length. One detail about the model: it reads the last context_length days of a series and silently ignores the rest.

On daily M5 data the longest history at the validation origin is 1,885 days, shorter than the documented 2,048 default and far shorter than the 8,192 maximum, so every series is read in full. On a finer-grained time grid the same 8,192 steps would be a much shorter span and the default would be quietly truncating most of the history.

Four prior checks I made

  1. Batching is not sharing. With cross-learning off, a series forecast alone and the same series inside a batch of 100 gives the same answer.
  2. The point forecast is the median. The library names the column predictions and computes it in a variable misleadingly called mean, whilst in truth it corresponds to the median.
  3. The context length changes nothing yet. Forecasting at the 2,048 default equals forecasting at the model maximum, since no history is that long.
  4. Quantiles ordered, no missing values. No missing values — but 19.1% of rows have at least one crossing quantile pair. It is worth knowing before reading any interval as… an interval.

Zero-shot

Show the code 
models = ["zero", "seasonal_naive", "moving_average_28d",
          "xgboost_btrotta", "chronos2_vanilla"]
md(rename_models(table_of(models, "validation"))
   .select(["model", "n_series"] + metrics.METRICS).sort("WMAPE"))
Show the code 
fig, axes = plots.plot_by_bucket(table_of(models, "validation", by="horizon_bucket"),
                                 metrics.METRICS)
plt.show()

Figure 1 shows the performances side by side of the out-of-the-box Chronos2 and the previously studied models.

The verdict is very clear: MAE and WMAPE drop by 10.3% against XGBoost, despite no specific features at all. This forces us to conclude that, at least empirically in this case, the engineering the gradient-boosted baseline needs — lags, rolling windows, per-weekday moments at three aggregation levels, etc — is handmade, and therefore too “crude”: reality doesn’t cleanly align with the dichotomies we create. On the contrary, Chronos-2’s training allowed it to build a much more subtle and complex net of operations, which we already knew excelled on problems it was optimized on. However here it had never seen this dataset before, and it is one we could describe as very “unusual”. The performances it just showed are that much more impressive.

We already justified at the end of the previous post that part of the 10.3% is the median-versus-mean advantage: XGBoost is trained on squared error and estimates a conditional mean, and on absolute-error metrics the median is the better point forecast regardless of which model is the better forecaster. Also P90 goes the other way: Chronos-2 is 3.8% worse than XGBoost on the bad days. According to a company’s priorities, there could still be a debate on which model to use.

Show the code 
def per_series(model, metric, role="validation"):
    return metrics.score(scored(model, role), by="id").select(
        "id", pl.col(metric).alias(f"{metric}_{model}"))

volume = (scored("chronos2_vanilla", "validation")
          .group_by("id").agg(pl.col("y").sum().alias("volume")))
comparison = (per_series("xgboost_btrotta", "WMAPE")
              .join(per_series("chronos2_vanilla", "WMAPE"), on="id")
              .join(volume, on="id"))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.5))
share = plots.index_plot(ax, comparison, "WMAPE",
                         "xgboost_btrotta", "chronos2_vanilla", order_by="volume")
plt.show()

But Figure 2 is once again to Chronos-2’s advantage: it has the lower WMAPE on 75% of series — and unlike the baseline’s win in the previous post, this one is not exclusively carried by the high-volume items. We can observe in the graph a fair match at the low-volume items, and a quick margin for Chronos2 as the volume goes up.

Four reasonable but inadequate ideas

Now that we saw the out-of-the-box performances, the natural follow-up question is: how can we make it better?

Every now gain for the gradient-boosted baseline came from handing it new metadata or information. Chronos-2 accepts extra inputs too, so the obvious move is to hand it similar new knowledge.

This idea isn’t unreasonable. Anything derived from the target’s own past should be redundant to a model that reads the history, but prices, SNAP days and events are genuinely exogenous and cannot be inferred from sales alone. Neither can the calendar be inferred: since Chronos-2 reads only the target values, it has no way of knowing whether a given day is Christmas or just another Monday. If it was reading many years of history, the model would pick up on recurrent special dates, but shifting ones (take Black Friday for example) will be impossible to pinpoint…

I tried four families of such metadata, and tested the models against the zero-shot one. I also experimented on three different ways to marker-sales days, so the model would get better on low-volume items. Finally, I compared activating cross-learning to the default model:

Show the code 
attempts = changes.filter(pl.col("model") != "zero-shot")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 0.45 * attempts.height + 1.2), sharey=True)
plots.plot_change_bars(axes[0], attempts, "WQL")
plots.plot_change_bars(axes[1], attempts, "WMAPE")
axes[1].set_ylabel("")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Let’s run over the results of Figure 3 block by block:

Known covariates, one block at a time, all lose. Calendar costs 0.36% of WMAPE, price 0.47%, SNAP and events 0.16%. Weekday and month are the clearest case of redundancy — they are recoverable from the timestamps the model already has — but price and SNAP are not, and they lose anyway. Only all four blocks together helps, by 0.54%, which is small enough that a single validation window of 473 series cannot distinguish it from luck.

Cross-learning is the worst single idea tried on the headline metrics: +0.85% WMAPE and +1.12% WQL. Letting the series of a batch attend to each other should help a thin series borrow from its neighbours; surprisingly, on this data it hurts.

RQL disagrees, and sharply: -5.61%, a clear improvement this loss function — over-prediction priced at four times under-prediction, scored on the point forecast. Though lack of improvement on other metrics Suggest that the forecast moved down in unjustified cases.

Every encoding of the long zero runs loses too. About 27% of history days sit inside a run of at least 14 consecutive zero-sale days while the item is on sale. I used three ways to point them out: a past-only binary covariate (one/off), a second multivariate target, and replacing the values with NaN so the model treats them as unobserved. The first two land at −0.08% WMAPE and +0.10% WQL; masking is the worst result in the study at +2.32% WMAPE and +1.99% WQL.

These eight runs unfortunately converge towards the same conclusion: with a foundation model feature engineering harms predictive power. It brute-forces a crude characterization onto a far subtler machinery. That is the opposite of an algorithm like XGBoost, where the more the better, because it simply never uses bad metadata, since gain optimisation is a greedy Way of building its decision trees.

What about uncertainty?

I also recorded the mean width of every run’s 20–80% band, on the theory that an input the model cannot turn into a rule makes it less sure before it makes it worse. A widening would be the signature of a useless input.

That is not what happened. 7 of the 8 attempts came back narrower than zero-shot while scoring worse — cross-learning narrowest of all, at -3.66%. The expected failure mode was hedging; the actual failure mode is confidence that is not earned. Only NaN-masking widened, by 11.3%, and it is also the one whose point forecast degraded most, which is at least self-consistent: when told that a quarter of the history is unobserved, the model both loses the information and admits it.

Are the long zero runs predictable at all?

Before building anything on top of a forecast of zero-sales periods (a type of two-stage model) it is worth asking whether they can be forecast at all.

Chronos-2 can forecast several related series jointly. So instead of configuring it for sales alone, I ran it for two channels per item:

  • sales, in units — the thing actually being forecast;
  • is_blank, a 0/1 binary flag signaling of this day is inside a long zero run (more than 14 days)

It returns a forecast of both for every day of the window. That gives two things to check: whether the blank channel is any good by itself, and whether it pushes the sales channel in the right direction.

By itself, it isn’t good. Here I calculated the precision, defined as the share of real blank days amongst the blank days predicted, and the recall, defined as the share of real blank days captured by the prediction. Over the validation window, 2,000 of 13,244 scored (series, day) pairs sit inside a real zero run. Let’s look at how the zero-shot model and the multivariate one perform on this task:

source days flagged precision recall
the is_blank channel, median ≥ 0.5 1,483 0.55 0.41
read off the zero-shot sales forecast 8,696 0.22 0.96

Neither is usable: the channel misses three fifths of the runs it should catch, and reading them off the sales forecast flags so many days that the flag means nothing.

The deeper problem is the second check. The extra channel is only worth having if a forecast zero run drags the sales forecast down. That is directly testable, by comparing two sales forecasts of the same item on the same day, from two runs differing in exactly one respect:

  • without the blank channel — Chronos-2 given the sales history and nothing else, which is the zero-shot run everything in this post is measured against;
  • with it — the same model, the same history, plus the blank-run channel alongside.

Keep only the days where the run’s own blank channel predicts a zero run, and every point should fall below the diagonal.

Show the code 
multivariate = experiment("blank_second_target_both_channels")
blank_median = (multivariate.filter(pl.col("target_name") == "is_blank")
                .select("id", "origin", "date", pl.col("q0.5").alias("blank_median")))
vanilla = pl.read_parquet(ARTIFACTS / "predictions" / f"chronos2_vanilla_{ROSTER}.parquet")

coupling = (
    on_validation(multivariate.filter(pl.col("target_name") == "sales")
                  .drop("target_name"))
    .select("id", "origin", "date", pl.col("y_pred").alias("second_target"))
    .join(blank_median, on=["id", "origin", "date"])
    .join(on_validation(vanilla).select("id", "origin", "date",
                                        pl.col("y_pred").alias("zero_shot")),
          on=["id", "origin", "date"])
)
fires = coupling.filter(pl.col("blank_median") >= 0.5)
x = fires["zero_shot"].to_numpy()
y = fires["second_target"].to_numpy()
n_fires = fires.height
share_above = float((y > x).mean())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.2))
limit = float(max(x.max(), y.max())) * 1.05
ax.plot([0, limit], [0, limit], color=plots.TEXT_COLOR, linewidth=1, zorder=3)
ax.scatter(x[y <= x], y[y <= x], s=9, alpha=0.30, color=plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR,
           edgecolor="none", label="blank channel pulled sales down (as intended)")
ax.scatter(x[y > x], y[y > x], s=9, alpha=0.45, color=plots.MAIN_COLOR,
           edgecolor="none", label=f"it pushed them up ({share_above:.0%})")
ax.set_xlim(0, limit); ax.set_ylim(0, limit)
ax.set_xlabel("sales forecast WITHOUT the blank channel (units)")
ax.set_ylabel("sales forecast WITH it (units)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, frameon=False, loc="upper left", markerscale=2)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

They do not. On 35% of those 1,483 days, knowing about the zero run made the model forecast more sales, not fewer. It is asserting “a long zero run is likely here” and “I now expect higher sales here than I would have without that knowledge” at the same time. Therefore the two channels are barely coupled, so the multivariate framing has no future.

Context length: the knob that matters

The context length is the single setting that decides how much history the model sees. More is not automatically better: a long context can dilute the recent behavior that drives the next few days, while the far horizon may need more of the past. And because the far horizon and the near horizon may want different answers, the sweep is scored by horizon segment, not overall.

The decision rule I chose is the following: for days 1–7 and for days 8–28 separately, keep the context with the lowest WQL. If the two differ, stitch — days 1–7 from one, days 8–28 from the other — with the boundary at the edge of the first horizon bucket rather than at a tuned value.

Show the code 
lengths = sorted(
    int(path.name.split("_")[1])
    for path in EXPERIMENTS.glob(f"context_*_{ROSTER}.parquet")
    if path.name.split("_")[1].isdigit() and "origin" not in path.name
)
segment = (pl.when(pl.col("horizon") <= 7).then(pl.lit("days 01-07"))
             .otherwise(pl.lit("days 08-28")).alias("segment"))
sweep = pl.concat([
    metrics.score(on_validation(experiment(f"context_{length}")).with_columns(segment),
                  by="segment").with_columns(pl.lit(length).alias("context_length"))
    for length in lengths
])

longest = max(lengths)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.5))
for name, colour in [("days 01-07", plots.MAIN_COLOR), ("days 08-28", plots.TEXT_COLOR)]:
    part = sweep.filter(pl.col("segment") == name).sort("context_length")
    reference = part.filter(pl.col("context_length") == longest)["WQL"][0]
    ax.plot(part["context_length"].to_numpy(),
            100 * (part["WQL"].to_numpy() / reference - 1),
            color=colour, marker="o", markersize=4, linewidth=1.5, label=name)
ax.axhline(0, color=plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR, linewidth=1)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("context length (days, log scale)")
ax.set_ylabel("WQL vs whole history (%)")
ax.legend()
plt.show()

The shape of Figure 5’s curve gives us the optimum. Below roughly 150 days the model is badly starved and the error rises steeply; above a few hundred it is flat to within a fraction of a percent. The best length is 1,099 days for the first week and 1,829 for days 8–28 — but neither is a point, it is a plateau: 33 and 31 lengths score within 1% of those winners.

Two more things say the same. The same selection rule run on WMAPE instead of WQL picks 1,288 for the early segment rather than 1,099 — the same flat region, a different point in it. And a CPU run and a GPU run of the sweep disagreed on the coarse-grid winner, yet still selected the same final pair.

Show the code 
choice = read_json("context_choice")
early, late = choice["early_context"], choice["late_context"]
from m5_chronos2.chronos2 import stitch

candidates = {
    "whole history": experiment(f"context_{longest}"),
    f"best single length ({late})": experiment(f"context_{late}"),
    f"stitch {early} -> {late}": stitch(experiment(f"context_{early}"),
                                        experiment(f"context_{late}"),
                                        choice["early_last_day"]),
}
md(metrics.compare({k: on_validation(v) for k, v in candidates.items()},
                   reference="whole history")
   .select(["model"] + [f"{m}_change_%" for m in metrics.METRICS]), digits=3)

So: a 46-length sweep, a selection rule fixed in advance, a stitch across two regimes — and the whole process removed 0.11% of WMAPE and 0.08% of WQL. Reading the entire history, which is what the model does if you tell it nothing, is within a tenth of a percent of the best configuration available. Remember, though, that in this setting no series was longer than 2,000 days, which is far from the maximum capacity of Chronos-2: on a different model, or with more history, the relationship between performance and context length could be strikingly non-monotonic.

LoRA for finetuning

Full fine-tuning would update 120M weights. LoRA (for low rank) freezes them and learns a low-rank correction to the attention matrices and the output layer — a few hundred thousand trainable parameters, which is what makes the run affordable at all. I used rank 8, learning rate 1e-5, 1,000 steps, effective batch 32.

The protocol keeps the fine-tune away from what it is scored on:

Show the code 
SPAN = 200                                  # days of history drawn, for scale only
window_starts = np.random.default_rng(0).integers(-SPAN, -56, size=6)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 2.6))
for start, end, colour in [(-SPAN, -28, plots.GRID_COLOR),
                           (-28, 0, plots.MUTED_TEXT_COLOR),
                           (0, 28, plots.MAIN_COLOR)]:
    ax.barh(0, end - start, left=start, height=0.5, color=colour, zorder=2)

for row, start in enumerate(window_starts):
    ax.barh(0.72 + 0.17 * (row % 2), 28, left=start, height=0.13,
            color=plots.TEXT_COLOR, alpha=0.55, zorder=3)
ax.text(-SPAN, 1.12, "random 28-day training windows", fontsize=8,
        color=plots.TEXT_COLOR, va="bottom")

ax.axvline(0, color=plots.TEXT_COLOR, linewidth=1.2, linestyle="--", zorder=4)
ax.text(0, 1.3, "forecast origin", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9,
        color=plots.TEXT_COLOR)
for x, text, colour, align in [
        (-SPAN / 2 - 14, "history\ntraining windows cut at random from here",
         plots.TEXT_COLOR, "center"),
        (-30, "−28 → 0\nvalidation target,\nscored every 100 steps",
         plots.TEXT_COLOR, "right"),
        (30, "0 → +28\nthe forecast window,\nnever touched",
         plots.MAIN_COLOR, "left")]:

Nothing else than intuition forces a model to forecast at the context length it was tuned at, so I tried all four pairings.

Show the code 
def lora(finetune_context, predict_context, origin):
    name = (f"lora_ctx{finetune_context}_steps1000_lr1e-05_bs32"
            f"_context_{predict_context}_origin{origin}")
    return experiment(name)

configs = {f"zero-shot, context {c}": experiment(f"context_{c}") for c in (early, late)}
for finetune_context in (late, early):
    for predict_context in (early, late):
        configs[f"LoRA@{finetune_context}, context {predict_context}"] = lora(
            finetune_context, predict_context, VALIDATION_ORIGIN)

by_segment = metrics.compare(
    {name: on_validation(table).with_columns(segment) for name, table in configs.items()},
    by="segment")
md(by_segment.select("model", "segment", "WQL").pivot(on="segment", index="model",
                                                      values="WQL"), digits=6)

Per-segment winners: fine-tuned at 1,099 and forecasting at 1,099 for days 1–7, fine-tuned at 1,099 and forecasting at 1,829 for days 8–28. So *cross pairing** between the fine-tuning context length and the one for predicting turns out helpful! However the margins are very small, and the gap between it and the next best configuration is in the fourth decimal of WQL.

What this adds up to

Out of the box, on data it had never seen, Chronos-2 beat a reproduced top-4% feature pipeline by 8.3% of WMAPE. Then the combined effect of greedy optimization on every axes yields a fraction of a percent, in the wrong direction on the point forecast. These results really highlight the power of the model’s architecture. It isn’t even a heavy-duty model with only 120M parameters, to be compared to GPT-3’s 175B parameters: and that was in 2020! However the posts also reveal a transformer’s shortcomings: past the out-of-the-box performances, only very meager gains can be made, if not none at all.

The flat part of that story is not a failure of effort. Every configuration I tried lands in the same narrow band, which is what a ceiling looks like from the inside. The honest next question is not “which knob did I miss” but “is this a limit of the tuning, or of the problem?” — and that one is answerable, which is what the third post does. It also weighs the one lever I never pulled: treat different series differently — fine-tune per group, cross-learn inside a group, one model per group. The possibilities there are endless, which is exactly why the question deserves an answer and some guidance instead of blindly testing as many models as our machines can take on.
